title: What we have touched (1 John 1:1–4)
hook: the elder writes of what he has seen, heard and touched

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of James, and the elders called to the bedside. Your line was going after someone who wandered.

You can read a whole biography of someone, dates, places, letters, photographs, and still not know the feel of their handshake, or how their voice sounded saying a name. Some knowing goes through the eyes and ears, and some goes through the skin. Today a new letter opens, called First John. It has no greeting, no name, no to-whom. It starts mid-breath, like a witness on the stand who can't wait to say what he knows. And the first thing he talks about is touch.

In the King James Bible: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life." The senses pile up. Heard. Seen. Looked upon, a word for gazing, taking it in. And then, handled: the word means to feel for something, the way you reach out in the dark. From the beginning echoes the first line of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word. For this writer, the Word of life is someone you could touch. Who's writing? The letter never says. Tradition says John the apostle, and the style is close to John's Gospel. Some scholars think it comes from a community shaped by that Gospel, and hear the same voice as the one who calls himself the elder in Second and Third John. Either way, he speaks as a witness: we were there, we saw, we touched. Why say it this way? Because some people, it seems, were teaching that Jesus only seemed to have a real body, a spirit wearing a costume. The writer answers with his own hands: we touched him; he was real flesh. Then the purpose: "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us." Fellowship is a deep word: sharing, partnership, a common life. Not a club. And the reason he's writing at all: "And these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full." Not to win an argument. So the joy can be full.

Put your hand on something near you, the table, a cup, your own arm, and feel its temperature, texture and weight; you don't have to believe it's there, you know it through your hand. Then let your mind move to one person whose hand you've held, and remember the feel of it. If you pray, give thanks for what is real and near.
Fellowship. First John's reason for writing at all, a deep word for sharing, partnership, a common life: so that your joy may be full.
Your line: joy made full. This letter begins with touch. That's day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 1:1–4 in the Christmas season, as a witness that the Word became flesh, and use the letter's opening when teaching about fellowship.

chat.says: Why does First John keep saying 'we touched him'? Isn't that kind of odd?
options: He's a witness: some taught Jesus only seemed to have a body, and he answers, he was real flesh.
He means touching the scroll's pages, because the Word of life is the written book itself.
He's describing healings, when sick people touched Jesus's robe and were made well again.
chat.meaning: Some, it seems, taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body. The writer answers as a witness: heard, seen, handled. He was real flesh.

First John.meaning: a New Testament letter that opens with no greeting or name

Word of life.meaning: the writer's name for Jesus, someone you could touch

the elder.meaning: how the writer of Second and Third John names himself

notes: The index hook says 'the elder writes'; 1 John itself does not name 'the elder' (2 and 3 John do). The script says 'a teacher later letters call the elder'. Confirm.
Authorship: tradition (Irenaeus and others) attributes the letter to John the apostle; many scholars posit a Johannine community. Both given, unranked.
The opponents' view (Jesus only seemed to have a body, later 'Docetism') is a common scholarly reconstruction; the script hedges with 'it seems'. Confirm.
Use of 1 John 1 in the Christmas season: e.g. readings for the feast of St John (Dec 27) in some calendars. Confirm howItsDone.
